did.abstract: The unrestricted papers consist of correspondence, news releases, clippings, and subject files from William F. Buckley's 1965 campaign for mayor of New York; and letters and scrapbooks concerning God and Man at Yale and his 1950 "Alumni Day Address."

bioghist.head: Biographical / Historical
bioghist.p: William F. Buckley, Jr. was born in 1925 and graduated from Yale University in 1950. In 1955 he founded the magazine The National Review . He also wrote a nationally syndicated column and hosted the weekly television show Firing Line from 1966 through 1999. In 1965 Buckley ran unsuccessfully as the Conservative Party candidate for mayor of New York City. From 1969 to 1972 he served on the Advisory Commission on Information of the United States Information Agency. He wrote numerous books including God and Man at Yale , espionage novels, and a trilogy based on his sailing expeditions. Buckley is considered one of the founders of the modern Conservative movement. Buckley died on February 27, 2008, at his home in Stamford, Connecticut.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The William F. Buckley, Jr. Papers consist of more than five hundred linear feet of material. Papers relating to the publication of God and Man at Yale , files from Buckley's 1965 campaign for mayor of New York City, and his 1950 "Alumni Day Address" are open for research. All other material is closed to research.

The Mayoralty Campaign, 1965 (boxes 293-326) is composed of material used in or collected for Buckley's campaign for mayor of New York City in 1965. Buckley ran unsuccessfully on the Conservative Party ticket against John Lindsay. There are several boxes of correspondence mainly composed of letters of advice and criticism and letters from campaign contributors. The section also contains news releases, newspapers clippings, and a large number of miscellaneous subject and research files relevant to issues in the campaign.

Boxes 410-414 contain letters and scrapbooks concerning Buckley's God and Man at Yale (New York, Henry Regnery and Co., 1951). In this book, Buckley charged that Yale taught collectivism and Keynesian economics and that the overall atmosphere at Yale encouraged agnosticism. The correspondence consists of approximately 450 letters, largely dated between 1951 and 1954, from the public, and exchanges between Buckley and his publisher. A list of correspondents is included in this register. The files also contain scrapbooks of articles about the book.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: Part I, Correspondence, following the arrangement of Mr. Buckley's staff, is divided into three sub-sections: General correspondence, 1954-1969; Author's file, 1965-1966, 1969; and General editorial file, 1966, 1969.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: General correspondence, 1954-1969. This is the largest section and includes both William F. Buckley's personal correspondence and the correspondence files relating to the operation of National Review . The correspondence is arranged alphabetically by the name of the writer or recipient of the letter for each year, except for the years 1954-1957, which are combined on one list. Additional correspondence of individuals may be found under corporate or subject headings; they have not always been cross-referenced. Some of these headings exist regularly, for example, those for Buckley's column, television program, speaking arrangements, and some organizations and publications, such as the Conservative Party of New York State, the Historical Research Foundation, the Young Americans for Freedom and the New York Times ; others occur only for special occasions, for example, National Review's Tenth Anniversary Book and Dinner in 1965, Buckley's candidacy for the Yale Corporation in 1967-1968, and various legal cases, political campaigns, trips and books. Occasionally, the folder titles change from year to year. Correspondence pertaining to Buckley's newspaper column, for example, is filed under "Adams Service" from 1962-1964 and under "Washington Star Syndicate" from 1965-1969. Whenever possible such changes have been cross-referenced. Correspondence about the publication of a book, lawsuit, or temporary organization covering more than one year has generally been kept together and filed under the most recent year, with appropriate cross-references. Family correspondence, filed under "Buckley family," appears only for the years 1962, 1968 and 1969. Other personal materials filed under William F. Buckley," such as "Art and artists," "Boat," "Charities and contributions" and "Personal business" -- do not occur in every year. Correspondence of National Review staff members referring to internal magazine matters has generally been filed under "Inter-Office Memos" or "Personnel." Correspondence written in behalf of Buckley or the magazine to non-staff persons is filed under the name of the correspondent. Additional personal correspondence of a staff member may be found under the name of the staff member. There is also some personal correspondence of Priscilla Buckley and William F. Rickenbacker with others for the years 1966 and 1969. From 1954 to 1962, the Mc's are filed separately after the Ma's and Mac's. From 1963 to 1969, the Mc's are interfiled with the Ma's and Mac's.

Author's file, 1965, 1966, 1969. This section includes the correspondence of Priscilla Buckley and the editorial staff with authors submitting material to National Review for publication. The correspondence of individuals, for whom there is also correspondence in the "General correspondence" section, has been removed and added to the latter section, with appropriate cross-references. The Author's file for 1965 also contains material not directly related to authors, such as letters to the editor and requests for information, which in 1966 and again in 1969 was filed in the "General editorial file" section

General editorial file, 1966, 1969. This section contains letters to the editor, suggestions, reader or "public opinion mail, requests, and other routine letters ordinarily answered by the editorial staff. Job applications, however, have been filed in "General Correspondence" under "Personnel."

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The William F. Buckley, Jr., papers, Part II, include all correspondence files from 1970 to 1979 as well as all subject files, writings, photographs and memorabilia received by Manuscripts and Archives through 1979.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: The papers were processed with funding, for one year, from Buckley. In order to complete the arrangement of this massive quantity of material in the time allowed, the papers underwent "light processing." The order within each series reflects the basic arrangement established by Buckley's office, and titles on folders have generally not been changed. Original staples have not been removed, and only the deteriorating items in Series I have undergone preservation photocopying. No attempt has been made to do in-depth subject analysis of the contents of these papers. Materials regarding the television program Firing Line in part of box 137 and all of box 138 have been removed from the collection.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The papers are arranged in four series: I. Correspondence, II. Subject files, III. Writings, IV. Photographs and memorabilia.

accessrestrict.head: Conditions Governing Access
accessrestrict.p: The following collection materials are open without restriction: Mayoralty campaign, 1965 (Part II, Series II, boxes 293-326) and God and Man at Yale (Part II, Series III, boxes 410-414).
Access to the material requires the written permission of Christopher T. Buckley during his lifetime, after which access is unrestricted.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Correspondence contains most, though not all, incoming and outgoing letters addressed to Buckley from 1970 to 1979. (For earlier correspondence see Part I and later accessions) Additional correspondence is filed by topic in Series II and III. The series is divided into two sections: General and Dan Oliver file. General contains most correspondence of note and is by far the larger of the two sections. Included in this section are letters from authors, business people, columnists and editors, foreign leaders, political figures, publishers, show people, and other high profile individuals. All correspondence in this section is addressed to Buckley or signed by him, though staff members may have drafted many of the outgoing letters. The section is arranged in alphabetical order by correspondent.

Frequent correspondents are listed by full name. All other correspondence is arranged in folders by letter. The files reveal some correspondence filed by subject, such as: "Buckley, W.F., Jr.-Boat;" "Convention, 1972;" "Old and young people;" "Speeches;" and "United Nations telegrams." Some office memoranda are filed under 'I' for interoffice rather than under the name of the individual staff members. Similarly some correspondence with members of the White House staff is filed under 'W' for White House rather than under the staff member's name. Unidentified correspondence will be found under 'U'. Many interesting letters from Whittaker Chambers and his family and from others concerning Chambers are filed under "Chambers, Whittaker Book." Copies of outgoing letters remain fastened to the incoming letters to which they pertain.

At the end of the section are three boxes which the Buckley National Review office, labeled "miscellaneous." This correspondence, received on February 5, 1980, was left in the chronological order in which it came (1970-1978). The folders contain interoffice memoranda, letters from readers of Buckley's columns, anonymous letters, invitations, thank you letters, newspaper clippings, and printed bulletins. Significant items were removed and placed in their proper place in the alphabetical file.

Dan Oliver file contains a file maintained by Oliver of correspondence which he handled for Buckley. Incoming letters are addressed to Buckley and outgoing replies are signed by him, though presumably the letters were drafted by Oliver. Most letters are from the general public, many from readers who wrote to disagree with Buckley's column or to complain about or praise a public stance taken by him. The file is arranged in alphabetical order by correspondent.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Five sections comprise this series, each section containing material relating to professional activities or interests. The sections are: Mayoralty Campaign, 1965; Trips, 1972; United Nations, 1973; USIA, 1968-1972; and Gore Vidal, 1968-1972. Each section contains correspondence and other pertinent material such as memoranda, printed matter, newspaper clippings, news releases, committee minutes, and transcripts of meetings. Some of this material is filed by topic as background or research files; other material is categorized strictly by type.

Mayoralty Campaign, 1965, is composed of material used in or collected for Buckley's campaign for mayor of New York City in 1965. Buckley ran unsuccessfully against John Lindsay on the Conservative Party ticket. There are several boxes of correspondence mainly composed of letters of advice and criticism and letters from contributors. The section also contains news releases, newspaper clippings, and a large number of miscellaneous subject and research files relevant to issues in the campaign. (Photographs from Buckley's debate with Lindsay are in Series IV.)

Trips, 1972, contains correspondence, newspaper articles, and other material concerning China, India, Israel, Russia, Vietnam, and the South Pole, places visited by Buckley in his travels in 1972. The material is arranged alphabetically by place.

United Nations, 1973, contains papers used as background during the three months Buckley served as the public member of the U.S. delegation to the 28th General Assembly of the United Nations. There is also material published by the U.N. such as summaries and transcripts of meetings which Buckley collected during his term.

USIA, 1968-1972, is composed of correspondence, memoranda, and printed material Buckley collected as a member of the United States Information Agency's Advisory Commission on Information to the U.S. Congress (USIA). The bulk of the section is USIA publications.

Gore Vidal, 1968-1972, is composed of papers created or collected for a lawsuit stemming from appearances by Buckley and Gore Vidal as commentators during ABC's coverage of the political conventions in 1968. During one broadcast Vidal called Buckley a pro-Nazi and Buckley accused Vidal of being a homosexual. Countersuits resulted, and when Esquire printed Vidal's story Buckley sued the magazine too. Esquire agreed to a financial settlement, Vidal's suit against Buckley was dismissed in Federal court, and Buckley eventually dropped his suit against Vidal. The papers in this section include correspondence, press releases, drafts, copies of newspaper articles, and clippings. Original folder headings were retained but the order of the folders was changed in order, where possible, to keep material on the same subject together.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Writings includes papers for Buckley's books, his column "On the Right," and for some speeches. The series begins with Books, which contains papers for fifteen of Buckley's books. The section is arranged alphabetically by book title, and for any particular book there may be manuscripts, galleys, memoranda, correspondence concerning publication or containing opinions from readers, and clippings. (Boxes 428-429 contain advance proofs and actual printed copies for twelve of these books.)

Copies of Buckley's column "On the Right" for National Review are arranged in chronological order. The Buckley office labeled the files from 1962-1968 as "drafts." These contain annotated typescripts. From 1969-1974, the files contain clean typescripts which the office labeled "original."

Speech material contains transcripts of broadcasts and other drafts concerning Buckley's speaking engagements. For additional information on speeches see Correspondence: General, Speeches 1970-1978. Accessions 2013-M-014 and 2013-M-042 include speech files for the years 1950-2007 and may consist of speeces, correspondence, and notes.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This accession consists of correspondence, subject files, writings, and memorabilia, the majority from later in his life. Correspondence is personal in nature and most of his correspondents were members of his family and friends; professional correspondence is generally filed within their related subject files and writings. Subject files include materials from organizations soliciting Buckley's support, newspaper and magazine clippings about Buckley, planning information for events held by Buckley, and materials related to controversies and lawsuits involving Buckley. A significant amount of materials are from the National Standard , the news magazine that Buckley founded, and the television debate show Firing Line , founded and hosted by Buckley. Writings comprise drafts and final copies of speeches, articles, and nonfiction books written by Buckley, including an unpublished book about his conflict with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). There are also some drafts of film screenplays based on novels written by Buckley. Materials date from 1950 to 2008, with the bulk dating from 1990 to 2008.
